title: The Band-Aid Paradox: Australia cannot recruit its way out of the teacher retention crisis
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes argues that Australia's energetic response to its teacher shortage treats symptoms rather than causes, trying to fill a leaking bucket without repairing the holes. Using Australian Teacher Workforce Data, she points to a 50-hour median working week, workload and wellbeing as the main reasons for leaving, and widespread insecure contracts for early-career teachers. She then identifies a second paradox: rapidly recruiting inexperienced and overseas-trained teachers adds mentoring load to the experienced staff the system most needs to keep. Wellbeing initiatives and financial incentives are treated as further Band-Aids, since they cannot fix structural workload and often just move vacancies between schools. Drawing on AITSL's 2025 wellbeing analysis, she contends the solution is to reduce job demands and strengthen resources such as professional agency. She closes with a concrete outline of a genuine retention strategy built around protecting teachers' time, induction and mentoring, behaviour support and listening to teachers.
points: Hughes cites a 50-hour median term-time week and that only 48 per cent of early-career teachers hold ongoing positions as evidence that retention, not recruitment, is the core problem.
Recruiting large numbers of new or alternatively trained teachers can worsen attrition by loading unprotected mentoring work onto experienced colleagues.
Mindfulness, resilience training and yoga are dismissed as unable to fix structural workload, echoing AITSL's finding that wellbeing requires reducing job demands rather than helping teachers cope.
Financial incentives without housing, workload relief and leadership support merely relocate shortages, so that the vacancy changes postcode while the national shortage remains.

Her retention blueprint treats teacher time as finite, removes tasks before adding new ones, guarantees trained mentors with protected time, and provides career progression that does not require leaving the classroom.
quotes: Each initiative is intended to bring more people into Australian classrooms—and many are worthwhile. But there is a problem. We are trying to fill a leaking bucket without repairing the holes.
This is the Band-Aid paradox. A Band-Aid is useful when an injury is small and temporary. It becomes dangerous when it allows us to pretend that a deeper wound has been treated.

We tell new teachers that they are entering one of society’s most important professions, then often offer excessive workload and insufficient support. We should hardly be surprised when some decide the bargain is not worth it.

When mentoring is bolted onto an already unmanageable workload, experienced teachers carry the cost. They plan, observe, reassure, explain, model and troubleshoot, often without protected time or specialist development. A policy designed to relieve workforce pressure can therefore create more work for the very people holding the system together.

Mindfulness, resilience training, yoga sessions and wellbeing afternoons may be appreciated. But they cannot compensate for persistent disruption, administrative overload, poor leadership or a working week that routinely expands beyond the hours for which someone is paid. You cannot breathe or downward-dog your way out of a structural workload problem.
Incentives can also move shortages around. One school gains a teacher because another loses one. One jurisdiction improves its staffing by offering more than its neighbour.
A genuine retention strategy would begin by treating teachers’ time as a finite and valuable resource. It would stop adding tasks without removing others.
